'''James Henry Harrison Jr.''' (born May 4, 1978) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Kent State Golden Flashes football|Kent State Golden Flashes]] and was signed by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2002. A five-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection, Harrison won two [[Super Bowl]]s with the Steelers: [[Super Bowl XL|XL]] and [[Super Bowl XLIII|XLIII]]. In 2008, he became the only undrafted player to be named [[Associated Press NFL Defensive Player of the Year]]. Harrison was known for his hard-hitting style during games.

Harrison also played for [[NFL Europe]]'s [[Rhein Fire (NFL Europe)|Rhein Fire]] and had brief stints with the [[Baltimore Ravens]] and [[Cincinnati Bengals]]. After the 2013 season, he stated that he would be retiring from the NFL, but he came out of retirement to return to the Steelers, and spent part of his final NFL season with the [[New England Patriots]]. Harrison ranks third on the Steelers' all-time sack leaders list, with 80.5. He currently appears on [[Fox Sports 1|FOX Sports 1]] as a football analyst.

'''James Joseph FitzPatrick, III''' (born February 1, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] for six seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Fitzpatrick was born in [[Heidelberg|Heidelberg, Germany]]. He began his football career in [[Beaverton, Oregon]] where he was a two way starter for the State Champion Beaverton High School Beavers.<ref name="PFR1">{{Cite web |title=James FitzPatrick Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FitzJa21.htm |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

He attended USC ([[University of Southern California|University Of Southern California]]),<ref name="PFR1"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Oates |first=Bob |date=1985-09-29 |title=FitzPatrick Says 'Little Things' Beating USC : Tackle Blames Fumbles and Interceptions, Still Believes in Running Game |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-09-29-sp-18891-story.html |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> where he played in the 1985 Rose Bowl against Ohio State, defeating them 20–17. As a senior, he was selected as the team's Offensive Player of the Year,<ref name="SBCS">{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=December 11, 1985 |title=USC Post Season Awards |work=[[The San Bernardino Sun|San Bernardino County Sun]] |quote=Also honored at Southern Cal's annual football awards banquet at the Bonaventure Hotel was offensive tackle James Fitzpatrick, the team's offensive player of the year}}</ref> and was named a first team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]].<ref name="GNS">{{Cite news |last=Buchsbaum |first=Joel S. |date=December 3, 1985 |title=Running backs, tackles take center stage |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/5310507/the_gns_allamerica_team/ |access-date=2024-12-21 |work=The Journal News (White Plains, NY)|via=Newspapers.com |page=C3}}</ref>

He was selected in the first round (13th overall) by the [[San Diego Chargers]] in the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref name="PFR2">{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-01 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played four seasons for the Chargers.<ref name="PFR1"/><ref name="LAT">{{Cite web |date=1986-07-26 |title=Chargers Sign FitzPatrick, Reach Terms With James |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-07-26-sp-145-story.html |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=Los Angeles Times|via=United Press International |language=en-US}}</ref> He was traded to the then [[Los Angeles Raiders]] in 1990 where he returned to the Colosseum for the remainder of his career.<ref name="PFR1"/>

James now lives in [[Portland, Oregon]], he is active in youth football.

'''James Weldon Hadnot''' (July 11, 1957 – March 30, 2017) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for four seasons for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  In his first two years of [[college football]] at [[Texas Tech]] Hadnot played tight end where he was a capable pass-catcher and solid blocker. In need of a running back, coach Rex Dockery switched his big receiver to fullback.  Running from the veer formation, Hadnot used his considerable size and surprising speed to rush for a school record 1,369 yards as a junior in 1978, then 1,371 yards as a senior, leading the Southwest Conference both years.  He was selected to the [[1978 College Football All-America Team]] (2nd team).  He was also chosen [[Southwest Conference]] offensive player of the year in both 1978 and 1979.

During his spectacular 1979 season at Texas Tech and in his subsequent Hula Bowl and Senior Bowl appearances, NFL scouts from the Kansas City Chiefs had taken notice of Hadnot's speed and power.  They made him their third round pick in the [[1980 NFL draft]].  In his rookie year he made a solid contribution alternating time with [[Tony Reed]] and [[Horace Belton]] at running back.  Hadnot took over the starting fullback position in 1981, leading the way for the dazzling [[Joe Delaney]] while contributing 603 yards rushing and 215 yards receiving of his own.  In addition to his four-year NFL career with the Chiefs, Hadnot caught 19 passes for 214 yards at tight end for the [[San Antonio Gunslingers (USFL team)|San Antonio Gunslingers]] of the USFL in 1985.

After retirement from football, Hadnot returned to his beloved college town of Lubbock where he resided until his death.  In 2005, he was enshrined in the Texas Tech Athletic Hall of Honor.

Hadnot died on March 30, 2017.<ref>[https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/lubbockonline/name/james-hadnot-obituary?id=9695955 James Weldon Hadnot]</ref>
